node-11.label: Peripheral vestibulocochlear disorder due to fat-containing lesion (likely lipoma) at the porus acusticus

why.why: The radiologist's analysis explicitly interprets the fat-containing lesion with soft-tissue enhancement on postcontrast fat-saturated T1 at the porus acusticus as likely lipoma with enhancing component, anatomically at the vestibulocochlear nerve entry. This direct expert interpretation supports the specific peripheral lipoma hypothesis, increasing confidence from 0.55 to 0.65. Confidence remains moderate because histopathology is not available and central pathology cannot be fully excluded without audiometry, vestibular function tests, and EEG.

node-12.label: Peripheral vestibulocochlear disorder due to vestibular schwannoma at the porus acusticus

why.why: The radiologist's analysis favors a lipoma with enhancing component at the porus acusticus. Although vestibular schwannoma is the most common enhancing tumor at this location and could explain the soft-tissue enhancement, the fat-containing nature of the lesion is atypical for schwannoma. The radiologist's interpretation makes schwannoma less likely, so confidence is reduced from 0.25 to 0.15.

node-13.label: Peripheral vestibulocochlear disorder due to meningioma at the porus acusticus

why.why: Meningioma can occur near the porus acusticus and enhance on MRI, but it is not typically fat-containing. The radiologist's interpretation of the lesion as likely lipoma with enhancing component makes meningioma less likely, reducing confidence from 0.15 to 0.10.
